opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think about it a lot. The short answer is that there are a few walls you hit at the same time.

The first is just raw computation. The world has an enormous number of degrees of freedom. If you want to simulate every molecule of air in a room, you're talking about something like 10 to the 27th particles, and no computer comes remotely close to that. So in practice we always have to coarsen things. We use continuum models, grids, particles that each represent huge numbers of real molecules. And the moment you coarsen, you've made a trade: you've given up some fidelity in exchange for being able to run at all.

The second wall, which people often underestimate, is memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic. Modern GPUs can do an incredible number of floating-point operations per second, but physical simulation is usually memory-bound. You spend most of your time moving data around: reading neighbor particles, writing grid values back. That's a big part of why I got interested in building Taichi, because how you lay out data and schedule computation matters as much as the algorithm itself. A lot of performance was being left on the table simply because writing high-performance simulation code was so hard.

The third is multiscale physics. Real phenomena couple across scales: turbulence has eddies spanning many orders of magnitude, fracture starts at the micro level and shows up macroscopically. A single resolution can't capture everything, and stitching different scales together robustly is still an open research problem.

Then there's time stepping. Many simulators are bounded by stability conditions like the CFL condition, so if anything in your scene moves fast or is very stiff, you're forced into tiny time steps. That alone can make a simulation thousands of times slower than real time even when the scene looks simple.

And finally, there's the question of whether we even know the right equations and parameters. For fluids and rigid bodies we're in good shape, but for things like biological tissue, granular media, or anything involving complex chemistry, the models themselves are approximate. So even with infinite compute, you'd be faithfully simulating a slightly wrong world.

What gives me optimism is that these limits are getting attacked from several directions at once: better hardware, better compilers and programming languages for simulation, and learned components that can approximate expensive parts of the physics. I don't think we'll simulate the entire world faster than real time anytime soon, but simulating the parts that matter to a particular question, fast enough to be useful, is becoming very realistic.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because "simulate the entire world faster than real time" is basically the dream behind everything I've worked on, from Taichi to the physics-based graphics research I did at MIT.

I'd break the limits into three layers, and honestly the hardware is the least interesting one.

The first layer is the sheer scale of the physics itself. The real world is doing something like Avogadro's number of interactions every nanosecond, and we're never going to brute-force that. So every simulator is really a hierarchy of approximations: we pick a resolution, a time step, a constitutive model, and we throw away everything below that. The question is never "can we simulate the world," it's "at what level of abstraction do the things we care about still emerge correctly." For fluids or snow or soft bodies, you can get visually and physically convincing results with MPM or SPH at resolutions that are many orders of magnitude coarser than molecules. But every time you want more fidelity, the cost grows superlinearly. Halve your grid spacing in 3D and you pay roughly eight times in memory and sixteen times in compute once you account for the smaller time step. That scaling law is brutal, and no GPU generation is going to repeal it.

The second layer, and this is where I spent most of my PhD, is that our hardware is actually pretty fast, but our ability to use it is terrible. A modern GPU has tens of teraflops sitting there, and most physics code uses a few percent of that. The reason is that physical simulation is memory-bound and irregular. Particles move, sparse grids get populated and depopulated, neighborhoods change every step. Writing code that keeps the memory hierarchy happy for that kind of workload is extremely hard, and it's a completely different skill from understanding the physics. That's really why I built Taichi. The observation was that the physicist and the performance engineer shouldn't have to be the same person, and the data layout should be decoupled from the algorithm so you can try ten different sparse structures without rewriting your solver. We got order-of-magnitude speedups in a lot of cases just by making it possible for people to actually experiment with that. So I'd say a big limiter is the programming model, not the silicon.

The third layer is the one I've become more convinced of over time: we don't actually know all the models. Simulation is only as good as the equations you feed it, and for a huge fraction of the world, we don't have clean first-principles equations. Friction, fracture, how a piece of fabric behaves after being washed a hundred times, how a human walks. Those are where differentiable simulation and learning come in. If you can backpropagate through your physics engine, you can fit the parts you don't understand from data and keep the parts you do understand as hard constraints. That hybrid is, I think, how we eventually get something that feels like a faithful world model rather than a very pretty cartoon.

So if you ask me what actually limits us today, in order: the fundamental cost scaling of resolution, then our inability to write software that saturates the hardware we already have, then gaps in our physical models. People tend to blame the first one and wait for Moore's law, but I think the second and third are where most of the leverage is right now. Faster than real time for a room, or a car crash, or a factory floor, is very achievable. Faster than real time for the whole planet at human-relevant fidelity is still a question of choosing the right abstractions rather than buying more chips.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental question is what level of detail you want to simulate. If you mean every particle and every interaction, then you have an enormous amount of information to represent and compute. And the computer itself is part of the world, so simulating everything faithfully becomes a very difficult proposition.

But usually we don’t need every detail. We want to capture the behavior that matters for a particular purpose. You can simulate some aspects of the world faster than real time by making approximations and ignoring things that don’t affect the result much.

So I would say the limits are both computational resources and our ability to find good approximations. How much can we simplify while still getting the right answer? That’s where better algorithms can make a big difference.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what level of detail you want to simulate. If you want to simulate every particle in the world, then the amount of computation is enormous. But usually, we don’t need every particle—we need a model that captures the behavior we care about.

For example, if you’re simulating water, you might care about the shape of a wave, but not the motion of every molecule. That approximation makes the problem much more manageable. So the limitation is partly computing power, but also our ability to find efficient representations and algorithms that preserve the important physics.

And then there’s knowing the initial state. Even if you had a very fast simulator, you wouldn’t know exactly what’s happening everywhere in the world. Small errors can grow over time. So running a simulation faster than real time and accurately predicting the real world are two different challenges.
